entries.seminar_title: Export Bans for Industrial Development: Evidence from Indonesian Nickel
entries.speaker: Patrick Farrell
entries.abstract: I study the consequences of Indonesia's nickel ore export ban. Manufacturing increased sharply following the ban, largely attributable to the entry of smelters. However, villages near new smelters saw declining public-goods provision, worsening infrastructure, and rising pollution, consistent with strain on local governments. While manufacturing output grew, this growth was entirely attributable to processed nickel products as other manufacturing output fell. I use export transaction records and firm ore purchase declarations to estimate a model of two-sided market power to decompose smelter margins into output markups and input markdowns. The ban's mixed record offers lessons for countries considering similar policies.

entries.seminar_title: Demobilization Through Inaction: Bureaucratic Delay, Ambiguity, and Collective Action
entries.speaker: Emily Sellars
entries.abstract: I present a theory of how bureaucratic inaction can defuse contentious political mobilization. By holding open the possibility that citizens can obtain demanded concessions through institutional channels eventually, authorities can create uncertainty about whether more radical actions are needed. This can reduce the incentives for mobilized backlash, but only when citizens retain sufficient optimism about the benefits of remaining patient. I assess the predictions of the model using data on Mexico's twentieth-century agrarian reform. Though this reform eventually resulted in the expropriation and redistribution of much of the country’s land area, it was carried out gradually and very unevenly over more than 80 years. Drawing on administrative data on land redistribution and original archival data on how petitions for land were processed, I present evidence that authorities often chose to keep pending cases open rather than granting any official response, positive or negative, and that ambiguity over the course of the reform indeed succeeded in defusing conflict. However, this strategy became less effective when and where the prospects for reform seemed either unusually promising or unusually discouraging and was less used where citizens' patience for waiting was plausibly lower. I conclude by considering the applicability of the theory to other settings and other types of reforms.

entries.seminar_title: Who Pays for Tariffs Along the Supply Chain? Evidence from European Wine Tariffs
entries.speaker: Felix Tintelnot
entries.abstract: We study how tariffs affect prices along the supply chain using product-level data from a large U.S. wine importer during the 2019-2021 U.S. tariffs on European wines. Combining confidential transaction prices with foreign suppliers, U.S. distributors, and retail prices, we trace tariff passthrough from producers to consumers. Pass-through at the border is incomplete, yet consumers paid more than the tariff revenue collected. The dollar markups per bottle for the importer contracted, but expanded for the combined distributor-retailer segment. Price changes along the chain reached consumers after one year. We also document tariff engineering that biases unit values in trade statistics.

entries.speaker: Eduardo Dávila
entries.abstract: This paper develops probability pricing, extending cash flow pricing to quantify the willingness-to-pay for changes in probabilities. We show that the value of any marginal change in probabilities can be expressed as a standard asset-pricing formula with hypothetical cash flows derived from changes in the survival function. This equivalence between probability and cash flow valuation allows us to construct hedging strategies and systematically decompose individual and aggregate willingness-to-pay. Four applications examine the valuation of changes in the distribution of aggregate consumption, the efficiency effects of varying performance precision in principal-agent problems, and the welfare implications of public and private information.

entries.seminar_title: Judge IV Designs with Multiple Treatments and Instruments
entries.speaker: Myunghyun Song
entries.abstract: Judge IV designs supply the randomly assigned judge as one discrete instrument, while with three dispositions the effect of a reform combines the effects at the margins it moves. Two-stage least squares with judge propensities generally involves all three margins at once and carries a bias from the margins it does not target. This paper constructs an instrument per treatment from the assigned judge and the case characteristics, letting each judge weigh the characteristics in their own way, with the distribution of the unobserved components unrestricted. Each margin effect is then reached from an outcome regression among the cases receiving a treatment and its derivative in the propensity. Revisiting recidivism in the Virginia Circuit Courts, a noncarceral conviction raises reoffending by less than reported, and incarceration raises it by at least as much, almost entirely in carceral form.
